extracted.intended_audience: students, translators, and scholars of Kantian philosophy (readers of the Critique of Judgement)
extracted.subtask_short: intro to kant critique of judgement
extracted.subtask_description: Prefatory introduction, translation notes, and glossary accompanying a translation of Kant's Critique of Judgement. Explains Kant's positions (on genius, aesthetic judgement, teleology, and Theism) and gives practical guidance on translation and editorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine Art is the Art of Genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine Art is regarded as the Art of Genius, 'that innate mental disposition through which Nature gives the rule to Art' (§ 46). Art differs from Science in the absence of definite concepts in the mind of the artist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great artists rarely can communicate their methods ('indeed he cannot explain them even to himself'). Poeta nascitur, non fit; genius is the faculty of presenting aesthetical Ideas—intuitions of the imagination to which no concept is adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius must be checked by Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant (via the author) holds that genius requires to be kept in check by taste: 'if in a work of art some feature must be sacrificed, it is better to lose something of genius than to violate the canons of taste.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-mastery expresses 'the sanity of true genius'—artistic freedom should not override established canons of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetical Idea as ineffable intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetical Idea is 'an intuition of the Imagination, to which no concept is adequate.' A great work of art affects us by exciting such ineffable Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More is present in great artistic productions than can be perfectly expressed in language; evaluative attention should note what transcends conceptual description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic judgement grounds in the subject (a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging beauty 'we invariably seek its gauge in ourselves a priori'; the aesthetical judgement involves 'a reference of the representation to the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies that judgments about beauty are grounded in subjective faculties rather than learned from nature; evaluators should recognize the role of the subject's a priori faculties when assessing aesthetic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of purposiveness (Zweckmässigkeit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes purposiveness 'ohne Zweck'—the purposiveness of a beautiful object not directed to an external end—and purposiveness as adaptation to definite ends (teleological purposiveness in organic life).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for purposiveness either by positing design (a Supreme Force) or by treating purposiveness as a subjective projection of our judging faculty; the contrast structures debates about natural teleology and aesthetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty may be judged 'as if' purposive
rubrics_metrics.description: We have to contemplate beautiful objects 'as if' they were purposive, though they may not be so in reality (the idealistic doctrine Kant favors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating natural beauty, consider whether perceived purposiveness is an objective feature or a necessary mode of our judgement; be cautious about inferring design from aesthetic judgement alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleological explanation for organized (organic) bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: In organized bodies (e.g., the growth of a tree) parts are 'thought as existing for the sake of the others and the whole'—operations of nature in organised bodies seem different from mere mechanical processes and require teleological explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of biological purposiveness should recognize that parts are intelligible only in reference to wholes; purely mechanistic accounts may be inadequate for explaining functional integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Mechanism and Technic
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant's fundamental distinction: Mechanism refers to mechanical processes, while Technic (purposive operation) refers to nature's purposive working—both are needed in scientific explanation but are conceptually distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should keep Mechanism and Technic separate when explaining natural phenomena; failure to respect this distinction risks conceptual confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Darwinian/mechanistic challenge to purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics argue (as by Kirchmann and others) that doctrines like Natural Selection explain the semblance of purpose on mechanical principles—order arises from disappearance of the disorderly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text acknowledges coincidences with modern science: some purposive-looking processes may be mechanistically explained, but Kant (as interpreted here) still holds that purposive operation in nature generally needs to be assumed; weigh mechanistic explanations case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Hylozoism
rubrics_metrics.description: Hylozoism (explaining purposes by a world-soul) is dismissed as self-contradictory because lifelessness (inertia) is essential to matter; talking of living matter is 'absurd' (p. 304).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt hylozoist explanations for purposiveness in nature; they are judged incoherent on Kantian grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spinozism reduces purposiveness to ideality but fails causal unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Spinoza's reduction of natural purposiveness to ideality (unity of inherence in one substance) 'does not give what we seek'—it supplies unity of inherence but not 'unity of causal dependence' needed to explain purposive unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using idealist accounts to handle purposiveness, test whether they actually supply a causal account of teleological unity rather than merely re-describing phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theism as the most satisfactory explanatory doctrine (regulative, not constitutive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theism represents natural purposes as produced by the Will and Design of an Intelligent Author; 'Teleology finds the consummation of its investigations only in Theology' (p. 311). But Kant treats the Idea of God as 'regulative, not constitutive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Theism may best render purposiveness intelligible for reflective judgement, one must not claim objective theoretical proof of God; theistic language functions regulatively to organize inquiry, not to constitute empirical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian limit: God as 'thing of faith' supported by Moral Argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant holds the existence of God to be a 'thing of faith'—the Moral Argument (practical Judgement) establishes the concept of a final purpose which we must ascribe to creation; faith is 'the moral attitude of Reason' necessary for highest moral final purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating philosophical claims about God, distinguish theoretical demonstrability (absent) from moral necessity (present); moral considerations can justify a practical commitment without converting it into theoretical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to infer other minds is reasonable but not demonstrative
rubrics_metrics.description: We infer minds of others by analogy to our own—this is convincing but not demonstrative; by Kantian standards such inference is valid for the reflective but not the determinant Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize limits of analogical inference: it is a rational, inductive extension of a known cause (mind as vera causa) but does not amount to logical proof; treat claims about other minds accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian caution: do not ascribe determinate predicates to the supersensible
rubrics_metrics.description: Kant argues we have no right to predicate attributes of the Mind of Deity because the power at the basis of Nature is 'utterly above definition or comprehension'; applying familiar predicates goes beyond legitimate province.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theorizing about supersensible principles, restrict claims to regulative or methodological roles rather than asserting determinate ontological attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation principle: preserve exactness over elegance; consistent English equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Translator's policy: render Kantian technical terms with consistent English equivalents to preserve exactness even at cost of clumsiness (e.g., preserve relation between 'Vorstellung' and 'vorstellen', use 'representation' consistently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a fixed mapping of key German terms to English equivalents throughout the translation rather than varying for stylistic elegance; note that this may make prose clumsy but preserves philosophical distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific rendering and typographic conventions for Kantian terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete choices: avoid rendering 'Kritik' as 'criticism' everywhere—use 'Critique' or 'criticism' appropriately; distinguish 'real' from 'wirklich', 'Hang' from 'Neigung', 'Rührung' from 'Affekt' or 'Leidenschaft', etc.; print 'Judgement' with a capital when it signifies the faculty and lowercase when it signifies the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply typographic and lexical conventions systematically (e.g., capitalizing 'Object' vs 'object' to distinguish Objekt from Gegenstand) and prefer 'purposive' for Zweckmässig to preserve connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practice: textual basis and notation of variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a principal German text (here Hartenstein) but note that Rosenkranz occasionally preserves better readings; indicate all important variants between editions at foot of page and enclose added notes in square brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/translators should state their base text, record significant variant readings, and clearly mark editorial additions; acknowledge assistance and list emendations transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary practice: supply a consistent list of Kantian term-equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a glossary of Kant's philosophical terms with single English equivalents listed (e.g., 'Anschauung; intuition', 'Begriff; concept', 'Zweckmässig; purposive').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the glossary to preserve precise relations between German terms and English renderings across the translation; accept some awkwardness in English for the sake of conceptual fidelity.
